voice: Lūyī, first of the siddhas, sings as a blunt teacher to a circle of seekers: a stark riddle to open (the body-tree, Death in the mind), plain commands in the refrain, a scoff at the samādhis, an urgent call, and a closing first-person testimony. The register is plain, spare, spoken English, with short imperatives and no hymn tone.

lines.en: The body's a [fine tree]{taruvara}; its branches are five.
Make it firm, and measure [great bliss]{mahasukha}.
Through pleasure and pain you're sure to die.
Let go of hope in the rules of practice, and the bond of desire.
Press close to the side of [emptiness]{sunyata}: hey, hold it near!
I sat with [dhamaṇa]{dhamana} and [camaṇa]{camana}, the two, as my seat.

couplets.kept: The tree, its five branches and Death entering the restless mind stay as bare images. 'Five' moves to the line end so five/mind give a slant rhyme for ḍāla/kāla, with 'fine' chiming inside. Death, not Time, as approved.
couplets.letGo: The full rhyme ḍāla/kāla softens to a slant rhyme. The particle vi stays untranslated, as in the accurate English.

couplets.kept: The refrain keeps its two commands and Lūyī's naming, short enough to come round the same each time. 'Measure' compresses 'take the measure of'; 'it' stays the unnamed thing made firm, as in the accurate English.
couplets.letGo: The māṇa/jāṇa rhyme is lost: nothing in the line rhymes honestly with 'know'. 'Learn' would chime with 'firm' but shifts the sense (see questions).

couplets.kept: 'Why' moves to the end for a full rhyme why/die answering kariai/mariāi, and a scoffing turn. 'Pleasure and pain' keeps the paired sukha dukha with alliteration. Impersonal 'one' becomes generic 'you'.
couplets.letGo: The neutral question 'why practise' becomes a sharper jab at the listener. The locative reading 'in pleasure and pain' and the plural 'they die' are not sung.

couplets.kept: The commands let go / hold near stay paired, and re is sung as 'hey' (the accurate English's bare-exclamation alternative) to keep the call's bite. 4a's two objects swap places so desire/near give a slant r-rhyme for āsa/pāsa.
couplets.letGo: The rhyme no longer falls on the source's own words, hope and near. 'Hey' drops the plural address that 'friends' made explicit. Both halves stay long, as the source's first half is.

couplets.kept: Lūyī's self-naming and the objectless 'seen' stay. Dhamaṇa and camaṇa sit side by side in source form, so their chime survives. 'Seen' moves to the end, making seen/seat an echo like the conjectured diṭhā/baiṭhā.
couplets.letGo: The printed baiṇa does not rhyme; the English echo leans on the baiṭhā conjecture flagged in the accurate English, and may be judged one step too far (see questions).

questions: Refrain (2a-2b): the parimāṇa/jāṇa rhyme is let go. One option would give it back: 'Measure great bliss and make it firm / Lūyī says: ask the guru, and learn' (firm/learn slant rhyme). It sings the flagged alternative in which great bliss is what is made firm, and it has 'learn' for jāṇa, which leans toward coming to know rather than knowing (Munidatta: jānīhi ... aharniśaṃ, cp.01.m3). I kept 'know'. If you take the option, the refrainCue becomes 'Measure great bliss and make'.

3b: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads bde ba rtsa nas bton na nges par 'chi, 'if bliss is pulled out by the root, one surely dies', and Munidatta's Sanskrit gloss has mahāsukhāvaghātena, 'through the destruction of great bliss' (cp.01.m4). Both point away from 'pleasure and pain'. The accurate English does not flag this, and I sang the line as it stands. Should the accurate line or its notes take it up?

4b: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads stong nyid phyogs la zhags pas bcing gis kye, 'bind (it) with a noose to the side of emptiness, kye!', taking pāsa as pāśa 'noose'. Munidatta's gloss also has nairātmadharmapāśa, 'the noose of the teaching of selflessness', next to samīpam (cp.01.m5). The accurate English's flags take pāsa only as 'near'. Should the noose reading be recorded?

4a: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has spongs shig sdeb sbyor byed cing g.yo sgyu'i blo, roughly 'give up the mind that makes verses and schemes'. It supports the chandas 'metre' (versification) alternative that the accurate English lists for chāndaka bāndha. I sang 'desire' as the accurate English has it.
4b: re is sung as 'hey' to keep the call short and sharp. If you prefer the plural address, 'Press close to the side of emptiness: friends, hold it near!' drops in without changing the rhyme.

Couplet 5: the English makes a seen/seat echo although the printed text (baiṇa) does not rhyme. This leans on the baiṭhā conjecture. Keep it, or unrhyme the couplet (e.g. 'Lūyī says: I have seen in meditation') to match the printed text?

1b: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sgra gcan 'Rāhu' in the line itself (g.yo ba'i sems la sgra gcan rab tu 'jug), carrying Munidatta's reading into the song. The accurate English's flag on kāla does not mention this. Worth a witness note there?
